query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: During high‐temperature exposure, degradation in the as‐built FCC Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA is governed by the segregation of reactive elements (primarily Al, Cr, and Ti) to grain boundaries and interfacial regions, which in oxidizing atmospheres drives the formation of a continuous, protective oxide scale that preserves mechanical integrity, while in reducing atmospheres the lack or reduction of such oxide formation leads to internal oxidation and degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with an FCC matrix that delivers notable strength and fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Perform a controlled high‐temperature exposure (700–900 °C) in two different gas atmospheres – one oxidizing (e.g., air or controlled O2 partial pressures) and one reducing (e.g., H2-containing) – comparing the baseline alloy with variants that have slight modifications to the Al, Cr, or Ti content to alter the segregation behavior at grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Constant high temperature (700–900 °C) for predetermined exposure times with identical gas flow rates and partial pressures; side-by-side comparisons of the baseline and compositional variants in both oxidizing and reducing atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions and second-phase interfaces where segregation of Al, Cr, and Ti controls the formation and adherence of the oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing environments, segregation of Al, Cr, and Ti promotes the in situ formation of a continuous, adherent oxide layer (e.g., alumina and chromia type) that protects the underlying FCC matrix. Under reducing conditions, the same reactive elements are less able to sustain a protective oxide scale (or the oxides may be reduced), leading to internal oxidation and compromised intergranular cohesion, thereby accelerating degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as‐built baseline, the alloy exposed to oxidizing conditions will develop a well-adherent, continuous oxide scale with minimal internal damage and will retain its mechanical properties, whereas in the reducing atmosphere, the baseline shows evidence of grain boundary/internal oxidation accompanied by measurable degradation in strength and fatigue behavior. Additionally, compositional variants that decrease the availability or segregation of the reactive elements will show poorer oxide scale quality in oxidizing atmospheres and enhanced degradation in reducing environments.
generation.baseline: The unmodified, as‐built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with its established FCC microstructure and performance characteristics.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for elevated temperatures (700–900 °C) and exposure durations sufficient for oxide-scale evolution; deviations may occur if the temperature or gas conditions fall outside regimes where segregation and oxidation processes dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative kinetics and the relative influence of each reactive element (Al versus Cr versus Ti) in facilitating grain boundary segregation and oxide-scale formation remain uncertain. Additionally, the precise threshold between protective and deleterious oxidation across varying oxygen partial pressures has not been firmly established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the baseline alloy and variants with slight reductions in Al, Cr, or Ti. Subject all samples to identical high-temperature exposures (700–900 °C) in both an oxidizing (air or controlled O2) atmosphere and a reducing (H2-containing) atmosphere. Use cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and focused ion beam (FIB) imaging to examine grain boundary chemistry, oxide scale thickness, composition, and adhesion, complemented by mechanical testing (e.g., tensile/fatigue tests) pre- and post-exposure.
measurements: Grain boundary and oxide scale composition and thickness (via SEM/EDS and XRD)
Mechanical property degradation (via tensile or fatigue testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the baseline alloy exposed to oxidizing conditions does not develop a continuous, adherent oxide layer correlated with segregation of Al, Cr, and Ti, or if compositional modifications that are engineered to alter segregation do not result in corresponding changes in oxide scale integrity and mechanical performance in either oxidizing or reducing atmospheres, then the hypothesis that grain boundary segregation of reactive elements governs degradation is falsified.

Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. Multi-component refractory elements-based alloys possess a mainly BCC structure. One of the most interesting HEA types is a system with coherent BCC and B2 phases with a microstructure similar to Ni-based alloys. The difference is that the disordered BCC phase is present as cubic nanoparticles. This structure provides a combination of high strength and high plasticity at high temperatures and is standard for Al-containing multi-component alloys. Thus, for the AlMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr alloy, its yield strength is 745 MPa at 1000 °C, and good plasticity is preserved (the height decrease is >50% under compression) []. However, there can also be observed oxides and intermetallic phases, such as Laves phases, in the refractory HEAs that can affect the materials’ ductility. For example, in the NbCrMoTaTiZr, CrNbTiZr, and CrNbTiVZr alloys, the Laves phase is formed in the BCC-matrix because of the smaller radius of Cr in comparison to other elements [,,]. Nevertheless, in Reference [], an NbMoTaWVCr alloy with an extremely high yield strength of 3416 MPa and good plasticity of 5.3% at room temperature was obtained. AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) have demonstrated excellent potential in various applications owing to the unique properties. One of the most critical issues of HEAs is the stress corrosion cracking (SCC) which limits its reliability in practical applications. However, the SCC mechanisms have not been fully understood yet because of the difficulty of experimental measuring of atomic-scale deformation mechanisms and surface reactions. In this work, we conduct atomistic uniaxial tensile simulations using an FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy as a typical simplification of normal HEAs, in order to reveal how a corrosive environment such as high-temperature/pressure water affects the tensile behaviors and deformation mechanisms. In a vacuum, we observe the generation of layered HCP phases in an FCC matrix during tensile simulation induced by the formation of Shockley partial dislocations from surface and grain boundaries. While, in the corrosive environment of high-temperature/pressure water, the alloy surface is oxidized by chemical reactions with water and this oxide surface layer can suppress the formation of Shockley partial dislocation as well as the resulting FCC-to-HCP phase transit

decision.trend: Earlier work on Al–Cr–Fe–Ni–Ti high-entropy alloys with an FCC-dominant matrix (PMC10095688, PMC10650386) has clarified how multi-principal compositions and heat treatments influence microstructure and mechanical strength. However, definitive insights into oxidation behavior under various elevated-temperature gas environments remain limited. In parallel, investigations of FeNiCuAl-based HEAs (PMC13208696) demonstrated how multi-element synergies, e.g., involving Cr and Co, can enable protective oxide formation, yet the complexity of these interactions (and how they shift during thermal cycling or when gas environments change from oxidizing to reducing) is still not fully resolved. The net outcome is that although compositional control can tune mechanical performance and oxidation resistance, there is no unambiguous mechanism describing how synergy among Al, Cr, Ti, and Ni–Co–Fe in FCC-phase HEAs causes either protective or deleterious reactions at elevated temperatures.
decision.unsolved: The precise mechanistic link between partitioning of reactive elements (Al, Cr, Ti) at grain boundaries, oxide nucleation sites, and oxide-scale evolution under different gas environments remains unclear. It is not yet certain whether minor changes in local composition coupled with phase evolution and interfacial reactions ultimately govern the integrity of the protective scale and alloy performance. These subtleties complicate the design of HEAs for sustained oxidative or reductive atmospheres at high temperature while preserving critical FCC-dependent ductility and fatigue strength.
decision.lever: Conduct a side-by-side high-temperature exposure of baseline Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples and variants with slightly shifted Al-Ti or Cr contents, under systematically varied oxidizing (air or controlled O2 partial pressure) vs. reducing (H2-containing) atmospheres at 700–900 °C. Track evolving microstructures, oxide scale chemistry, and mechanical properties using a combination of XRD and cross-sectional electron microscopy at incremental exposure times.
decision.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that the interplay of Al, Cr, and Ti at grain boundaries and second-phase interfaces controls the formation and adherence of stable protective oxides in different gas conditions, thus affecting high-temperature degradation. Monitoring changes relative to the as-built FCC microstructure will reveal how local composition, phase evolution, and environment-driven reactions contribute to scaling or other forms of damage. Observing a persistent protective oxide layer on the baseline composition across a range of oxygen partial pressures and temperatures would support the hypothesis, while accelerated internal oxidation or intergranular attack in variants with altered Al-Cr-Ti content (or in a reducing environment) would falsify it.
